Peptides are everywhere right now. I was at the gym talking to my buddy Jeff, who asked me what my “peptide stack” was. I’m like, “My peptide stack?” Neither one of us was actually taking peptides, but he’d heard so much about them that he was curious. And that’s exactly what’s happening right now. You open Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube, and somebody is talking about peptides, weight-loss drugs, recovery, anti-aging, muscle building, or some new biohack that’s supposedly going to change your life. There’s so much hype that I think we need to understand what peptides actually are before we start injecting random sh*t into our bodies.

The first thing you need to understand is that peptides aren’t magic—they’re messengers. Peptides are small chains of amino acids that essentially send instructions to your body. Think of them like text messages: regulate appetite, release growth hormone, repair tissue, or perform some other specific function. A peptide isn’t testosterone, and it isn’t a steroid. Different peptides send different messages, which means they can have different benefits and risks. The second thing you need to understand is that just because something is called a peptide doesn’t mean it’s safe. Everything you put into your body can potentially have risks and side effects. One of my biggest concerns is where people get this stuff. There are shady websites selling compounds as “research chemicals,” and you may have absolutely no idea whether what you’re buying is sterile, properly dosed, or even what the label claims it is. If you’re considering something like this, I believe you need legitimate medical oversight, appropriate testing, proper dosing, and ongoing monitoring—not some dude on the Internet promising you a shortcut. And that brings me to probably the most important point: peptides will not fix a bad lifestyle. Everybody wants the shortcut. We want to lose fat faster, recover quicker, look younger, build muscle, sleep better, and feel incredible. But a recovery peptide doesn’t replace sleep, and something designed to support performance doesn’t replace actually going to the gym. These things can potentially support a plan, but they cannot replace the fundamentals—exercise, nutrition, sleep, consistency, and taking care of your body.

Before I would ever consider taking a peptide, I’d ask myself:

What problem am I actually trying to solve? Don’t take something simply because your buddy is taking it.

Is there legitimate research showing that it actually works? TikTok testimonials aren’t scientific evidence.

Am I getting it through a legitimate medical provider? Where it comes from, how it’s administered, and how you’re monitored matter.

Do I understand the risks and potential side effects? There is no free lunch when it comes to this stuff.

Have I fixed the basics first? If your diet sucks, you don’t exercise, and you’re looking for a magic bullet, you’re probably wasting your time, money, and energy.

At the end of the day, I don’t think peptides are inherently good or bad. They’re tools. The right peptide, for the right person, for the right reason, with legitimate medical supervision, could potentially be incredibly effective. But don’t get sucked into the hype and start experimenting with your body because some jacked dude on social media told you it changed his life. Do your homework, understand the risks, fix the fundamentals, and if you decide to explore peptides, do it intelligently and under proper medical supervision.

I’ve always been paranoid about losing my hair because male pattern baldness absolutely runs rampant in my family. Both grandfathers, my uncles, my cousins—bald. So about five years ago, when I started noticing more hair in the drain, on my pillow, and in my brush, I freaked out. My hairline was changing, my widow’s peak was disappearing, and I was thinning around the crown. I knew I needed to do something.

I threw everything at it. I tried minoxidil, finasteride, and a red-light therapy cap. Unfortunately, minoxidil irritated my scalp and made my hair feel greasy, while finasteride caused sexual side effects almost immediately. That was a deal breaker for me. I stopped both, but I wasn’t about to stop looking for ways to protect my hair. The big thing I learned is that for a lot of guys, hair loss is connected to DHT, or dihydrotestosterone. DHT can attach to susceptible hair follicles and gradually cause them to miniaturize. The hairs become finer and weaker until eventually they stop growing. That’s why one of the most important lessons I can give you is this: don’t wait until your hair is gone to start caring about it. The earlier you notice thinning and take action, the better opportunity you have to preserve what you’ve got.

Because traditional treatments didn’t work for me, I started researching other options and working with labs and chemists in the hair-care industry. That ultimately led to the development of Pete & Pedro Boost Hair Growth Oil, which I use to support a healthy, hydrated scalp. I also realized I wanted a shampoo designed specifically for thinning hair and scalp health, which led us to develop DHT Defense Shampoo with ingredients including saw palmetto, pumpkin seed, pygeum, rosemary, caffeine, biotin, and niacin. These products became part of my routine because I wanted options beyond finasteride and minoxidil.

But products are only part of the equation. I also got serious about scalp health. I use a shampoo brush to gently massage and clean my scalp, helping remove oil, dead skin, styling-product buildup, and other junk. And after shampooing, I always use a hair conditioner. Shampoo and conditioner perform two different jobs, which is exactly why I’m not a fan of 2-in-1 products. Shampoo cleans; conditioner replenishes, smooths, and strengthens hair. I also don't use cheap, low-quality hair products, and I treat my hair like something worth protecting. I switched to a silk pillowcase because it pulls and tugs less on my hair while I sleep, and I added a hair supplement to my routine. I personally use Nutrafol. It’s definitely not cheap, but I’m willing to invest in taking care of my hair.

The biggest takeaway from my experience is simple: take action early. I caught my thinning when my hairline was just beginning to change, and instead of ignoring it and hoping for the best, I did something about it. You have multiple options—from improving your hair and scalp routine to medications and, for guys who need or want it, hair transplantation. The right solution will be different for everybody. At the end of the day, your hair is your responsibility. If keeping it matters to you, educate yourself, pay attention to changes, and start taking care of it before you’re staring at a bunch of hair in the drain wondering what the hell happened. I was genetically dealt a pretty crappy hand when it comes to hair loss, but I decided I wasn’t going to sit around and do nothing. It's your hair and your responsibility, so take action asap.

The supplement industry would love for you to believe you need a cabinet full of powders, pills, and potions to build an amazing body. You don’t. I’ve been working out for over 30 years; I used to own nutrition stores, and I’ve tried just about every natural supplement imaginable. What I’ve learned is that supplements can absolutely help—but they’re there to supplement the work, not replace it. If your diet sucks, you’re not training consistently, you’re sleeping like crap, and you’re not taking care of yourself, save your money.

No supplement can outwork a bad lifestyle. Get your ass in the gym, eat right, sleep, hydrate, and be consistent. Then, once you've got those fundamentals handled, supplements can help you get a little more out of the work you're already doing. And most importantly, do your own research and figure out what actually makes sense for you. That said, a handful of supplements are worth the money if you’re trying to build muscle, get leaner, improve performance, support healthy hormone levels, and ultimately build a better body.

Protein powder is at the top of my list because getting enough protein every day can be tough, especially if you’re trying to build or preserve muscle. I personally shoot for around one gram of protein per pound of body weight, and protein powder makes hitting that target quick and convenient. But remember—it's a supplement to real food, not a replacement.

I’m also a big believer in omega-3 fatty acids. Your body and brain need healthy fats, and getting enough omega-3s while cutting back on crappy fats can be an important part of a healthy diet.

Another supplement I use is psyllium husk, a source of soluble fiber. For me, it has helped with cholesterol, and because fiber helps keep you feeling full, it can also make staying within your calorie target easier.

For hormone support, I take a testosterone-support formula. My testosterone was 833 the last time I had it checked, but I’m not claiming a supplement caused that number. I simply like the ingredients and have been taking the product for over a year. This is also where supplement quality matters—you need to know and trust the company making what you're putting into your body.

Then there’s creatine, which I think is one of the biggest no-brainers for guys who train. I started taking it consistently about a year ago, and I currently use a creatine product that also includes MBP for bone-health support. Building a better body as we get older isn’t simply about looking muscular—it’s about staying strong, capable, and healthy for as many years as possible.

I’ve also been experimenting with Peak ATP to support workout energy and performance.

For workout energy, I keep things incredibly simple: caffeine. I love black coffee before training because it gives me energy without needing some crazy pre-workout. But you need to use caffeine responsibly. More isn’t better, especially if you're getting anxious, jittery, or screwing up your sleep.

Another one I love is citrulline because it supports nitric oxide production and blood flow. For workouts, that means better pumps and vascularity—which, come on, is freaking awesome when you're lean.

I also group vitamin D, zinc, and magnesium together because they’re important micronutrients involved in things like hormone regulation, immune function, and overall health.

Last is L-carnitine, which I’ve taken for years and like when I’m trying to get lean, especially with fasted cardio. But once again, none of these supplements magically burn fat, build muscle, or give you an amazing body while you sit on the couch. The foundation is always training, nutrition, sleep, hydration, and consistency.

I personally shoot for around one gram of protein per pound of body weight, and protein powder makes hitting that target quick and convenient. But remember—it's a supplement to real food, not a replacement.
I’m also a big believer in omega-3 fatty acids. Your body and brain need healthy fats, and getting enough omega-3s while cutting back on crappy fats can be an important part of a healthy diet.

Another supplement I use is psyllium husk, a source of soluble fiber. For me, it has helped with cholesterol, and because fiber helps keep you feeling full, it can also make staying within your calorie target easier.

For hormone support, I take a testosterone-support formula. My testosterone was 833 the last time I had it checked, but I’m not claiming a supplement caused that number. I simply like the ingredients and have been taking the product for over a year. This is also where supplement quality matters—you need to know and trust the company making what you're putting into your body.

Then there’s creatine, which I think is one of the biggest no-brainers for guys who train. I started taking it consistently about a year ago, and I currently use a creatine product that also includes MBP for bone-health support. Building a better body as we get older isn’t simply about looking muscular—it’s about staying strong, capable, and healthy for as many years as possible.
I’ve also been experimenting with Peak ATP to support workout energy and performance.

For workout energy, I keep things incredibly simple: caffeine. I love black coffee before training because it gives me energy without needing some crazy pre-workout. But you need to use caffeine responsibly. More isn’t better, especially if you're getting anxious, jittery, or screwing up your sleep.

Another one I love is citrulline because it supports nitric oxide production and blood flow. For workouts, that means better pumps and vascularity—which, come on, is freaking awesome when you're lean.
I also group vitamin D, zinc, and magnesium together because they’re important micronutrients involved in things like hormone regulation, immune function, and overall health.

Last is L-carnitine, which I’ve taken for years and like when I’m trying to get lean, especially with fasted cardio. But once again, none of these supplements magically burn fat, build muscle, or give you an amazing body while you sit on the couch. The foundation is always training, nutrition, sleep, hydration, and consistency.

The ultimate Toronto Chinese food tour with https://www.youtube.com/@InstaNoodls — 4 stops, from decades-old Cantonese BBQ in Chinatown to fiery chili oil noodles in North York, ending at Canada's FIRST Hakka Chinese restaurant!

Toronto is home to one of the largest Chinese communities outside of Asia, but most people don't realize how vastly different each neighborhood eats. Joined by Toronto food insider Clement Leung, we're going on a fast-paced 40-minute food marathon to uncover dishes you can't even find in China. We start with crisp Cantonese barbecue and legendary roast meats at New Hong Fatt B.B.Q., taste handmade Northern-style dumplings rolled right by the front door at Yummy Yummy Dumplings, brave a bowl of fiery bowl-seared chili oil noodles at 7 Noodles in North York, and finish at Yueh Tung, Canada's historic first Hakka restaurant, where two sisters are preserving their family's legendary recipe for Indian-Chinese chili chicken!

items.text:
Kabuli Pulao — the national dish of Afghanistan! Today in Kabul we're watching Afghanistan's most famous dish made from start to finish, plus chopan lamb kebabs, hand-churned Afghan ice cream, and the original Afghan burger.

Afghan food is one of the most underrated cuisines in the world, and today my friend Bilal Kamal is taking me to eat some of the best of it in Kabul, Afghanistan. The main event is Kabuli Pulao — mountain-sized rice cooked with tender lamb, sweet carrots, and raisins — and at Abid Pulao Restaurant we see the entire process from start to finish before digging in. Then we try an original Afghan fast food: the Afghan burger at Osman Burger, a flatbread stuffed with fries, salad, and chutney. We cool down with Sheer Yakh at Ghazna Ice Cream — Afghan ice cream hand-churned for 2 hours — and finish with what I'd been waiting for all day: sizzling bone-in chopan lamb kebabs at a Turkmen restaurant!

items.summary: Afghan food is a meat lover's paradise — from a legendary slow-simmered breakfast in Kabul Old City to a riverside lamb feast in Paghman Valley, just 45
items.text:
Afghan food is a meat lover's paradise — from a legendary slow-simmered breakfast in Kabul Old City to a riverside lamb feast in Paghman Valley, just 45 minutes from the city at the base of the Hindu Kush mountains!

Afghanistan's meat obsession is real, and today my friend Bilal Kamal and I are experiencing it from morning to night. We start in Kabul Old City with kalla pacha at Faizi Kalla wa Pacha Restaurant — slow-simmered sheep's head and trotters that just might be one of the world's greatest breakfasts. Next, hot out of the tandoor oven, we eat samsa — flaky Afghan baked meat pies — at Samarqand Sambosa Tandoori. Then we drive to the base of the Hindu Kush mountains to Paghman Valley, where locals escape the city for rivers, fresh fruit, lush green trees, and incredible food. Sitting riverside at Hamesha Bahar, we finish with rosh — fall-apart lamb stew cooked with potatoes and onions — for the ultimate Afghan countryside feast!

Then we drive to the base of the Hindu Kush mountains to Paghman Valley, where locals escape the city for rivers, fresh fruit, lush green trees, and incredible food. Sitting riverside at Hamesha Bahar, we finish with rosh — fall-apart lamb stew cooked with potatoes and onions — for the ultimate Afghan countryside feast!
